newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil awaits Iraqi flows to replenish US tanks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil awaits Iraqi flows to replenish US tanks.

text.p: Oil prices steadied on Wednesday, caught between news of falling gasoline supplies in the United States and the possibility that Iraq may more than double its oil exports next month from levels achieved earlier this year.

Brent crude oil, the world benchmark grade, closed one cent higher at $18.40 a barrel on the London futures market. Prices have fallen about 28 percent this year but are holding above a recent $17.32 a barrel 13-month low.
Despite the prospect of Iraqi barrels gushing into the market in August, supplies appear less plentiful in the short-term, oil traders said.
U.S. Government figures released on Wednesday showed fall in gasoline stocks of nearly four million barrels last week.
This helped keep a floor under prices despite bearish news from the United Nations that Iraq must stick to the letter of United Nations conditions for the continuation of limited oil exports.
Iraq was allowed by a U.N. resolution effective from June 8 to renew its deal to sell $2 billion of oil to fund food and humanitarian aid, in two $1 billion increments every 90 days.

But exports have stalled since then as the two sides discussed details of a new food distribution plan. That is now expected to be passed to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan for final approval next week, U.N. officials said.
Western diplomats at the U.N. said late on Tuesday that Iraq would only be allowed to carry over about five percent of the first $1 billion into the second 90-day period.

That requirement would mean Iraq, having delayed for two months the restart of exports, would have to sell oil at a much higher rate in August than was previously reckoned, or forego some of its oil sales receipts under the scheme.
"The Iraqi news is obviously very bearish for the market," said John Toalster, oil analyst at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull Securities in London.
"There is excess supply coming on to the market already," he said.

Assuming oil sales do not begin again until the last week of July, at the earliest, Iraq would then have about 40 days in which to sell around $1 billion of oil, or more than 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) at current prices unless the rules are altered, diplomats said.
By comparison Iraq sold about 660,000 bpd during the first 180-day period from December 10, 1996 to June 7, 1997.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see Iraq close to that 1.5 million bpd level for a short period," said Mehdi Varzi, oil analyst at Kleinwort Benson Securities in London.

Also putting downward pressure on the market is Germany's plan to sell 2.8 million barrels of crude oil from stocks. The sale is due to start in the week beginning August 4, which might coincide with the first Iraqi sales.

But lower Norwegian oil output next month due to oil field maintenance and a shut-in at a big Colombian oil field due to rebel attacks would "partially offset" the impact of higher Iraqi exports, Varzi added.
